Ashwood — a timeline of the invented county

Crafted fixture text. Every entry below is made up for this test fixture.

Year 1. The ash trees along the river are recorded as a boundary marker in a land
description that survives only as a copy of a copy.

Year 14. The bridge is built. The building is paid for by a levy on market traders, which
is the earliest sign of the arrangement the charter later formalises.

Year 22. A dispute between the miller's household and the reeve's household over the
grinding of grain is settled by an agreement that no longer survives.

Year 31. The charter is written, on the evidence of the handwriting and of the names in
its opening list. No date appears in the document itself.

Year 44. A second hand adds the clause forbidding the felling of the ash trees. The
addition is undated and its reason unrecorded.

Year 58. A third hand writes a complaint in the margin about the conversion of fines from
shillings into labour days. This is the last addition to the document.

Year 90. The market is recorded as meeting three days a week, which suggests the
after-harvest promise had become permanent.
